name: Latvia

facts.religion: Lutheran about 20%, Catholic about 20%, Orthodox about 18%, many unaffiliated

snapshot: Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs's United List won a record 41 of 100 seats in the October 2026 election and now governs with the nationalist National Alliance, as a party opposed to aiding Ukraine entered parliament.
culture: Latvia's Song and Dance Festival, held every five years, is a huge national event and, along with the dainas, short folk songs, was key to the "Singing Revolution". Midsummer, Jāņi, is the most important holiday, with bonfires and wreaths. Riga has Europe's largest collection of Art Nouveau buildings.
society: About a quarter of the population is ethnic Russian, and the government has phased out Russian-language schooling. Latvia spends heavily on defence and has reintroduced conscription. Emigration has shrunk the population since 1991. Forestry, logistics and IT are key sectors.
situation: Andris Kulbergs of the centre-right United List became prime minister in May 2026. In the 3 October 2026 election, on a record-low turnout of about 52 percent, his party won 41 of 100 seats with about 35 percent, the best result for any party since independence. On 17 November the Saeima approved his second government, a coalition of the United List and the nationalist National Alliance with 51 seats, by 57 votes to 34, with several nonpartisan ministers and a career diplomat, Girts Jaunzems, as foreign minister. It promises 2.875 billion euros in savings by 2030, continued support for Ukraine and severing economic ties with Russia and Belarus. The pro-Russian Sovereign Power, with 15 seats, is in opposition.
power: A parliamentary republic. The prime minister leads the majority in the 100-seat Saeima; the president is elected by parliament.

story: German knights conquered the Latvian lands in the 13th century, and Riga became a Hanseatic city. Latvia was independent from 1918 until the Soviet occupation of 1940, which brought deportations and mass Russian settlement. It regained independence in 1991 and joined NATO and the EU in 2004.

leader.who: Andris Kulbergs, prime minister, presenting his second government to the Saeima
leader.text: “They say you can't step into the same river twice. Well, I'm stepping in a second time.” He called record-low turnout “a warning to all of us.”

press.text: Led on the seven hours of debate before the vote, including criticism of the rushed process, the male-dominated cabinet and 'nonpartisan' ministers who are Kulbergs's former classmates or colleagues.

abroad.who: OSW, the Polish Centre for Eastern Studies
abroad.text: Saw a more cohesive government than in the last term, but one whose one-seat majority leaves it dependent on parts of the opposition, notably Ainars Slesers's Latvia First.
